items.text: REFERRED TO INVESTIGATIONS AND GOVERNMENT OPERATIONS
AMEND (T) AND RECOMMIT TO INVESTIGATIONS AND GOVERNMENT OPERATIONS
COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO RULES

items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5031

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the executive law, in relation to preventing housing
discrimination against victims of domestic violence; to amend the
executive law, in relation to prohibiting employers from
discriminating against victims of domestic violence or stalking in
seeking treatment or safety planning; to amend the family court act,
in relation to requiring law guardians to receive training or
education in domestic violence; to amend the domestic relations law,
in relation to requiring the court to state on the record the domestic
violence and child abuse factored into their award of custody or
visitation; to amend the penal law, in relation to providing that a
second violation of an order of protection within five years
constitutes the felony of criminal contempt in the first degree; to
amend the criminal procedure law and the family court act, in relation
to orders of protection; to amend the criminal procedure law, in
relation to reporting domestic violence incidents to the supervising
probation department or the division of parole; to amend the criminal
procedure law, in relation to certain history related to charges for
certain domestic violence offenses not be sealed; to amend the penal
law, in relation to the sentencing of a violent felony offender who
was a victim of domestic violence to a lesser determinate term; and to
amend the executive law, in relation to domestic violence fatality
review teams


 PURPOSE :

This bill would: (1) prohibit discrimination against victims of
domestic violence in employment and housing; (2) require four hours of
education and training on the effects of domestic violence for
court-appointed attorneys for children; (3) require courts to state on
the record how established incidents of domestic violence and child
abuse factored into determinations of visitation or custody; (4)
authorize concurrent jurisdiction in family court for certain sex
offenses; (5) provide for transmission of domestic violence incident
reports involving probationers or parolees to the relevant agency as
soon as practicable; (6) provide that a record of the termination of a
criminal action or proceeding by way of a conviction of harassment in
the second degree against a member of the same family or household
shall not be sealed; (7) allow for an alternative determinate sentence
where a court determines that domestic violence was a contributing
factor in the defendant's crime; and (8) allow localities to establish
domestic violence fatality review teams.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 of the bill would amend Executive Law § 292 of the Executive
Law to define the term "victim of domestic violence."

Sections 2, 3, 4 and 5 of the bill would amend various subdivisions of
Executive Law § 290 to prohibit discrimination in housing on the basis
of an individual's status as a victim of domestic violence.

Section 6 of the bill would amend Executive Law § 2% by adding a new
subdivision 20 to: (1) prohibit discrimination in employment on the
basis of a victim's status as a victim of domestic violence; (2)
require an employer, unless it would be an undue hardship, to provide
a reasonable accommodation to a victim of domestic violence, limited
to solely to allowing an absence, charged to leave or unpaid, for
certain activities set forth in the subdivision; (3) provide that an
employer is required to provide such a reasonable accommodation unless
it would pose an undue hardship to the employer; and (4) require an
employee who must be absent from work pursuant to this section to
provide reasonable advance notice, except where such notice is not
feasible.

Section 7 of the bill would amend Family Court Act (FCA) § 249-b to
require the chief administrator of the courts to promulgate rules to
provide that each person appointed to be an attorney for a child shall
complete at least four hours of training on domestic violence, the
effects of domestic violence on children and the relationship between
domestic violence and custody, visitation and child support.

Section 8 of the bill would amend Domestic Relations Law § 240(1)(a)
to require that, where allegations of domestic violence or child abuse
are raised and established by a preponderance of the evidence, a court
must state on the record how findings, facts and circumstances of
domestic violence or child abuse factored into the court's
determination of custody or visitation.

Section 9 of the bill would amend Penal Law § 215.51(c) to provide
that an individual is guilty of the crime of criminal contempt in the
first degree when he or she has violated any part of a duly served
order of protection.

Sections 10, 11 and 12 of the bill would amend Criminal Procedure Law
(CPL) § 530.11(1), FCA § 812(1) and FCA § 821(1)(a), respectively, to
add the crimes of sexual misconduct, forcible touching,sexual abuse in
the third degree and sexual abuse in the second degree as set forth in
Penal Law § 130.60(1) to those family offenses fur which a victim may
obtain an order of protection in family court, and subjecting these
offenses to mandatory arrest and reporting requirements of CPL §
140.10.

Section 13 of the bill would amend CPL § 140.10(5) to provide that a
report of a domestic violence incident for an individual known by the
involved law enforcement officer to be under probation or parole
supervision must be transmitted by the officer to the supervising
probation or parole agency as soon as practicable.

Section 14 of the bill would amend subdivisions 1 and 2 of CPL §
160.55 to provide that where a criminal conviction is terminated upon
conviction of a violation of harassment in the second degree committed
against a family or household member, the record of such conviction
shall not be sealed.

Section 15 of the bill would amend Penal Law § 60.12 to authorize an
alternative determinate sentence of imprisonment upon conviction of
certain crimes where domestic violence was a factor in the defendant's
crime. '

Section 16 of the bill would amend Executive Law § 575 by adding a new
subdivision 11 to: (1) allow a county, city or local government to
establish a domestic violence fatality review team to analyze certain
domestic violence-related deaths or near deaths, with the goal of
improving systems and facilitating communication among agencies; (2)
require that at least one representative of law enforcement or a
district attorney's office, one representative of a local department
of social services, and one representative of a domestic violence
services provider or advocacy group be a part of such a team; (3)
authorize such teams to access certain records, subject to
confidentiality protections; (4) provide that records, reports and
other documents received, made and maintained by such a team are
confidential and not subject to disclosure except by court order; (5)
provide that members of such teams are immune from civil and criminal
liability for reasonable and good faith actions taken in connection
with a team; and (5) require reporting to the Office for the
Prevention of Domestic Violence (OPDV) and periodic reporting by OPDV
to the Governor and the Legislature.
Section 17 of the bill would provide that it will become effective 90
days after enactment.

 EXISTING LAW :

Executive Law § 292 defines terms used in the Human Rights Law.

Executive Law § 296 sets forth unlawful discriminatory practices in
employment, housing, places of public accommodation, and other areas.

FCA § 249-b requires the chief administrator of courts to promulgate
court rules prescribing workload standards for attorneys for children.

Domestic Relations Law § 240(1) requires that, with respect to child
custody or visitation determinations in matrimonial actions, where
allegations of domestic violence or child abuse are established by a
preponderance of the evidence, courts must consider the effects of
such domestic violence or child abuse in making the custody or
visitation determination.

Penal Law § 215.51(c) provides that an individual is guilty of the
crime of criminal contempt in the first degree when he or she is
guilty of criminal contempt in the second degree and has violated that
part of a duly served order of protection which requires the defendant
to stay away from the person or persons on whose behalf the order was
issued.

CPL § 530.11 provides that criminal court and family court shall have
concurrent jurisdiction over certain crimes, including, for example,
disorderly conduct, harassment, menacing and stalking, when the crime
is committed between members of the same family or household.

FCA § 812 provides that family court and criminal court shall have
concurrent jurisdiction over certain crimes, including, for example,
disorderly conduct, harassment, menacing and stalking, when the crime
is committed between members of the same family or household.

FCA § 821 provides that a family offense proceeding may commence upon
the filing of a petition alleging, for example, that a respondent
engaged in certain criminal conduct against a household or family
member, including, for example, disorderly conduct, harassment,
stalking, menacing.

CPL § 140.10(4) provides that a law enforcement officer must arrest an
individual where the officer has reasonable cause to believe he or she
has committed an offense enumerated in CPL § 530.11(1) against a
member of the same family or household.

CPL § 140.10(5) provides that a law enforcement officer must prepare
and file a written report of a crime between members of the same
family or household, whether Or not an arrest is made.

CPL § 160.55 provides that, where a criminal action or proceeding has
been terminated against a defendant by way of the defendant's
conviction of a traffic infraction or violation, other than certain
enumerated violations, records of such criminal action or proceeding
shall be sealed.

Penal Law § 60.12 allows for an alternative indeterminate sentence of
imprisonment where a court finds that the defendant was the victim of
domestic violence, and such domestic violence was a factor in causing
the defendant to commit the crime.

 JUSTIFICATION :


Domestic violence is a crime of enormous magnitude that affects all
New Yorkers regardless of age, race, or economic status-with long term
and pervasive consequences for victims, families, communities and
society. Each year, an estimated 400,000 domestic violence incidents
are reported to law enforcement in New York, approximately 300,000
calls are received by hotlines throughout the State, and nearly
165,000 orders of protection were issued in domestic violence cases in
family, criminal and supreme courts in 2007 alone.

In New York and around the nation, several high profile domestic
violence cases have renewed focus on the effects of domestic violence
on its victims, children and our communities.  In addition, some
studies have indicated an increased risk of abusive conduct during
difficult financial times. The stresses of an economic downturn might
also make it more difficult for victims of domestic violence to feel
that they are able to take the steps they need to get and stay safe.

While New York vigorously responds to domestic violence, with over 550
police departments, 200 emergency rooms, 150 domestic violence service
providers, 99 domestic violence hotlines and 1,000 specialized courts,
improvements can be made to hold offenders accountable, support
victims of domestic violence and protect our children from exposure to
and involvement in domestic violence situations. This bill will
implement legislative changes that will strengthen New York's support
for victims and their children while holding offenders accountable.

*  PREVENTING; DISCRIMINATION AGAINST VICTIMS OF DOMESTIC VIOLENCE IN
EMPLOYMENT AND HOUSING

Stable housing and employment are often the most important resources a
domestic violence victim needs in order to stay safe. Often, it can be
challenging for victims to obtain and maintain housing as they may be
viewed by landlords as problem tenants due solely to the abuse they
suffer at the hands of another. It can also be difficult for victims
to obtain and maintain employment due to the stresses of domestic
violence, the abuser's interference with their ability to perform in
the workplace or their need to access services that are necessary for
their safety.  By including victims of domestic violence as a
protected class in the housing and employment provisions of the Human
Rights Law, the State will ensure that victims will not be prevented
from obtaining or maintaining housing or employment merely as a result
of their status as victims of domestic violence.

In addition; the proposal allows employees a reasonable accommodation
in taking time off to, for example, seek medical attention or
counseling or appear in court on matters related to incidents of
domestic violence, including child protective proceedings, unless time
off would constitute an undue hardship for the employer.  Employers
would have the option of requiring that employees charge this time to
accumulated leave credits or, where such leave credits are
unavailable, take unpaid leave.

*  PROTECTING CHILDREN FROM HARMFUL EXPOSURE TO DOMESTIC VIOLENCE

Children exposed to domestic violence often suffer psychological,
behavioral or academic challenges. In 1996, the legislature recognized
the harmful effects of domestic violence on children and established
domestic violence as a factor that courts must consider in child
custody and visitation proceedings. Thirteen years later, studies
indicate that the presence of domestic violence often has little
impact on custody and visitation determinations. This proposal would
require courts to state on the record how the findings, facts and
circumstances of domestic violence or child abuse were factored into
the custody or visitation determination, where such abuse was
established by a preponderance of the evidence. In addition, this
proposal would require that attorneys for children be trained on the
dynamics of domestic violence so they can better counsel and represent
their clients.

*  HOLDING OFFENDERS ACCOUNTABLE

Under the Penal Law, offenders face heightened sanctions for
violations of orders of protection when they violate the "stay away
from the person" provision of such an order. This bill will allow the
criminal justice system to appropriately elevate charges from a
misdemeanor to a felony for individuals who continually violate any
provision of an order of protection. This will protect victims who,
for instance, have an abuser who repeatedly threatens them from jailor
threatens them through a third party.

New York recognizes certain crimes as offenses that may be committed
within a family setting, and enumerates those offenses in FCA § 812:
When a crime is recognized as a family offense, victims are eligible
to petition for orders of protection in family court. These orders of
protection are listed on a state-wide registry and the police must
arrest an individual where there is reasonable cause to believe that
the individual has committed a designated family offense, Currently,
New York does not include sex crimes within those designated as
"family offenses," although there is a high correlation between
domestic violence and sexual assault. This proposal would allow
evidence of certain sex crimes committed against members of the same
family or household to be heard in family court order of protection
proceedings, while ensuring that mandatory arrest applies and that
orders of protection are filed with the statewide registry.

Law enforcement is not currently required to notify supervisory
agencies, such as probation or parole, when a probationer or parolee
is involved in a domestic incident. Law enforcement officers are
required to complete a domestic incident report when they respond to
any domestic call. This bill would require the law enforcement officer
to transmit a domestic incident report to probation or parole when the
alleged abuser is known to be on probation or parole. Since both of
these supervising agencies frequently impose the condition that a
probationer or parolee report any contact with law enforcement, this
proposal will assist the agencies in enforcing this condition, thereby
ensuring that offenders are held accountable.

Most domestic violence cases are initially charged as misdemeanors,
but many are ultimately plead down to harassment charges, which are
violations and subject to sealing. The process of sealing these
convictions provides an incomplete history of abuse, crucial to
charging decisions, such as course of conduct and primary aggressor.
This bill would allow a defendant to obtain a non-criminal
disposition, when all parties deem that outcome to be appropriate,
while ensuring that law enforcement has a complete understanding of
the nature of the domestic violence history for any future incidents.

*  STRENGTHENING PROTECTIONS AVAILABLE TO VICTIMS AND REMEDIES
AVAILABLE TO INCARCERATED VICTIMS

Pursuant to the Penal Law, domestic violence victims who are convicted
of violent crimes where domestic violence was a contributing factor
are how able to receive a reduced indeterminate sentence. Currently,
no defendants are incarcerated under this sentencing structure. This
proposal would authorize a court to sentence such a victim to a lower
determinate sentence, in accordance with modern sentencing structure.

Often, domestic violence-related fatalities and near-fatalities occur
after the victim, the victim's family, and the abuser, have accessed
the services of governmental entities and community services. This
proposal would allow localities to establish domestic violence
fatality review teams to review such fatalities or near-fatalities to
improve systems and reduce the number of deaths attributable to
domestic violence. Members of such review teams would be immune from
civil and criminal liability for reasonable and good faith actions
taken as a result of participation in such a team.

 BUDGETARY IMPLICATIONS :

This bill is not expected to have a significant impact on State
finances.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This bill would take effect ninety days after it becomes a law.

Section 9 of the bill would amend CPL § 170.10(4) to add a new
paragraph (e) to provide that the Court inform the defendant that the
records and papers in the arrest and prosecution of a conviction of
harassment in the second degree against a member of the same family or
household shall be accessible for law enforcement purposes.

Section 10 of the bill would amend CPL § 160.55(2) to provide that
when a defendant has been found guilty of harassment in the second
degree against a member of the same family or household, the clerk of
the court shall include notification of such disposition to the
Division of Criminal Justice Services.

Section 11 of the bill would amend CPL § 170.10 by adding a new
subdivision 8-a to provide notice to a defendant that he or she was
alleged to have committed harassment in the second degree against a
member of the same family or household and creates a procedure for
determining if the offense was committed against a member of the same
family or household.

Section 12 and 13 of the bill would amend CPL § 530.12(5) and CPL §
530.13(4), respectively, to provide that, upon conviction of a class A
misdemeanor and issuance of an order of protection, such order of
protection may be extended during the period of the defendant's
incarceration.

Section 14 of the bill would provide that, consistent with available
resources, the Division of Human Rights shall develop training
programs in conjunction with the Office for the Prevention of Domestic
Violence to implement certain changes to the Human Rights Law.

Section 15 of the bill would provide that it shall take effect 90 days
after enactment; however sections 7, 8, and 10 would take effect in

orders of protection in cases other than family offenses.
